title: String Memory Structure
concept: C has no 'string type'. It just uses a character array with a 0 at the end.

steps.title: Including stdio.h header
steps.explanation:
Standard I/O header for using `printf`.

This lesson examines how strings are stored as `char` arrays.

steps.title: Starting main function
steps.explanation:
The main frame is created.

We will see step by step how a string literal is placed into an array.

steps.title: Declaring a string as a char array
steps.explanation:
`char str[] = "Code";` creates an array with 4 characters plus the null terminator `\0`.

So the actual array size is 5.

steps.title: Printing the string (%s)
steps.explanation:
`%s` prints characters until it encounters `\0`.

That is why only the text portion of `str` appears as a normal string.

steps.title: Checking total array size (sizeof)
steps.explanation:
`sizeof(str)` returns the total byte count of the array.

Since the return type is `size_t`, the format specifier `%zu` is used.

steps.title: Examining array contents directly
steps.explanation:
Printing each element by index reveals the null terminator value (0) at the end.

The key point is that strings end with an invisible `\0`.

steps.title: Program termination
steps.explanation:
The program ends with `return 0;`.

Key point: When a string literal is copied into an array, the null terminator is included.

quiz.question: Why is char buf[5] = "Hello"; dangerous?
options: There is no room for the trailing \0, so it is not recognized as a string
quiz.explanation:
"Hello" has 5 characters, but requires 6 slots including `\0`.
Forcing it into `buf[5]` means there is no end marker, so printing will read past the buffer into adjacent memory (the start of Buffer Overflow).

misconceptions.wrong: You can get the string length with `sizeof`
misconceptions.correct: In most cases, you should use `strlen`.
misconceptions.why: `sizeof` returns the total size of the container (array), while `strlen` returns the actual content length (up to `\0`).

keyTakeaway: In C, a string is a `char` array ending with `0`. Always remember the `+1` slot.
